# Close Reading of the Opening of *Autobiography of a Yogi*

## 1. Scene by Scene

The text divides into two distinct sections: a front matter apparatus followed by the autobiographical narrative proper.

**Front Matter**: The edition announces itself as an online version with ALLCAPS marking former italics, footnotes collected at chapter ends, and illustrations provided in a zip file. The Contents and List of Illustrations have been moved before the Preface and Acknowledgements. A frontispiece of Paramhansa Yogananda is referenced (py.jpg). The title page lists Yogananda as author, with W.Y. Evans-Wentz (Oxford scholar and comparativist of Tibetan texts) providing a Preface. The Dedication to Luther Burbank frames the book as an American-Indian bridge. A map of India is promised (map.gif).

**Preface by Evans-Wentz**: The Oxford scholar recounts meeting Sri Yukteswar Giri at Puri in Orissa, describing him as "tall, straight, ascetic," with "long and somewhat curly" hair, "muscularly firm, but slender" body. He records that Yogananda was sent to the West in 1920 as Sri Yukteswar's "emissary," and records his own witnessing of the guru's passing in 1936.

**Author's Acknowledgments**: Yogananda credits Miss L.V. Pratt (editorial labor), Miss Ruth Zahn (index preparation), C. Richard Wright (travel diary extracts), and Evans-Wentz ("suggestions and encouragement").

**Chapter 1—My Parents and Early Life**: The chapter opens with Yogananda's claim of "clear recollections" from "a previous incarnation"—a yogi in Himalayan snows—establishing reincarnation as foundational to the text's worldview. He describes his 1890s birth at Gorakhpur as the "second son and fourth child" of eight siblings, with parents Bhagabati Charan Ghosh (mathematician and logician at Bengal-Nagpur Railway, Kshatriya caste) and his mother (devotee of Lahiri Mahasaya). A striking anecdote: the father, offered ten rupees to help a needy woman, initially refuses with a story of his own youth poverty, then yields with the line "You win!"—the "immemorial gesture of vanquished husbands." Father is revealed as a disciple of Lahiri Mahasaya, who organized Calcutta Urban Bank but refused shares, and who once neglected to claim 125,000 rupees in overdue bonuses. Mother is described as teaching "only through love," offering open-handed charity. A childhood episode: Yogananda, around age eight, falls sick with Asiatic cholera, and his mother urges him to bow mentally to Lahiri Mahasaya's photograph on the wall; a "blinding light" envelops him and he recovers instantly, with both him and his mother seeing the luminous phenomenon. Father tells the story of becoming a disciple: employee Abinash Babu asked for leave to visit his guru; Father ridiculed the plan; then, walking together, Lahiri Mahasaya "materialized" in a field, said "Bhagabati, you are too hard on your employee!"—and Father became a convert. Yogananda reports a childhood vision of Himalayan yogis in a flash of light, hearing the voice "We are the Himalayan yogis" and a subsequent vision of Iswara as Light. A scar on his right forearm is traced to an incident where, after arguing with sister Uma about a boil, he concentrated and willed a boil onto his own arm to prove his word-power, saying "By the power of will in me, I say that tomorrow I shall have a fairly large boil in this exact place." The boil appeared, was lanced, left a scar. Another anecdote: in Lahore, Yogananda and Uma watch kites from a balcony; he prays silently for two kites belonging to players across the lane; both kites come to him, looped by a cactus plant, and he gives them to a disbelieving Uma. The chapter closes with his receiving a photograph of Lahiri Mahasaya from Father, a photograph that had been impossible to take (the plate showed nothing where Lahiri Mahasaya sat) until the master "posed" willingly, then never again.

**Chapter 2—Mother's Death and the Mystic Amulet**: Mother dies while Yogananda is at Bareilly; her greatest wish had been to see eldest brother Ananta married. A midnight vision of Mother warns him; Father dismisses it as hallucination. Mother dies; the marriage is postponed. Yogananda returns to Bareilly and makes daily pilgrimages to a sheoli tree, observing strange lights. A cousin's tales of Himalayan saints reawaken his longing. He attempts to run away to the Himalayas with a landlord's son, Dwarka Prasad; elder brother Ananta "ridicules" him: "Where is your orange robe? You can't be a swami without that!" The attempt fails. Fourteen months after mother's death, Ananta delivers her deathbed message: she had been told by a sadhu that her "stay on earth will not be long" and that she would be custodian of a silver amulet, to be materialized in her hands during meditation, then passed to Ananta for one year, then to Mukunda. The amulet, covered with Sanskrit characters, was to come to Yogananda "about the time he is ready to renounce all worldly hopes." It vanished from Ananta's keeping, as the sadhu had prophesied, and Yogananda's receipt of it brought "a blaze of illumination" and "dormant memories."

**Chapter 3—The Saint with Two Bodies (Swami Pranabananda)**: Yogananda, age twelve, is sent by Father to Benares with a letter of introduction to Swami Pranabananda (Father's "brother disciple"). Father also has business with Kedar Nath Babu. Yogananda arrives and Pranabananda greets him with clairvoyance ("Are you Bhagabati's son?") before Yogananda can produce the letter. The swami explains he enjoys "two pensions"—one from Father (for his railroad work) and one "from my Heavenly Father" (the "fathomless peace" of deep meditation). He falls silent, Sphinx-like. Yogananda learns that Kedar Nath Babu will arrive in half an hour—then Pranabananda asks to be left alone. The man arrives; Yogananda learns that Pranabananda had appeared to Kedar Nath at the Ganges bathing ghat, told him of Yogananda's presence, then "dashed swiftly past" and disappeared, outpacing the man despite wearing wooden sandals. The explanation: Pranabananda had "materialized an extra body." The swami reveals he meditated eight hours nightly for eight years but always found "a little veil" between himself and the Infinite until Lahiri Mahasaya interceded: "I have interceded for you with Brahma." Afterward, the veil dissolved. Pranabananda obtained a railroad pension by telling the doctor his spine had an "overpowering sensation," and was freed for "unbroken communion with the Beloved."

**Chapter 4—My Interrupted Flight Toward the Himalaya**: Years later, Yogananda (now a youth in Calcutta at 4 Gurpar Road) plans a flight to the Himalayas with friend Amar Mitter, needing a hackney carriage to avoid detection. He packs a bundle of blanket, sandals, Lahiri Mahasaya's picture, Bhagavad Gita, prayer beads, and two loincloths, throwing it from his third-story window. He and Amar buy English clothes in Chadni Chowk to disguise themselves. They are joined by cousin Jotin Ghosh (Jatinda). At Burdwan, Jatinda vanishes with the shared money. Yogananda wants to return home ("This trip is doomed to failure") but Amar chides him: "Can't you stand the little test of a treacherous companion?" They continue. A European station agent questions them; Amar poses as "Thomas," son of an English mother and converted father, and Yogananda as "Thompson." The telegram from Ananta is read: "Three Bengali boys in English clothes running away from home toward Hardwar via Moghul Serai. Please detain them." Amar's brother and Ananta intercept them. At Benares, a pundit and his son try to dissuade Yogananda from renunciation; he cites the Bhagavad Gita (IX:30-31): "Even he with the worst of karma who ceaselessly meditates on Me quickly loses the effects of his past bad actions." A saint outside the pundit's house tells Yogananda, in response to his silent prayer, "Your sole path in this life is that of the renunciate." Father sends Swami Kebalananda as Sanskrit tutor; Yogananda learns the youth is a disciple of Lahiri Mahasaya. Kebalananda recounts his ten years with the master, describing Lahiri Mahasaya's half-closed eyes, his omniscient "clavis" for the Vedas, his practice of having disciples interpret scripture while he guided their thoughts. He tells of a blind disciple, Ramu, healed by Lahiri Mahasaya touching his forehead at the point between the eyebrows and telling him to chant "Rama" for seven days.

**Chapter 5—A "Perfume Saint" Displays His Wonders**: At Kalighat Temple, Yogananda meets a sage who speaks of Maya, duality, and the "savage" inward battle against delusive thoughts. The sage predicts an "unusual experience." Yogananda encounters Gandha Baba ("Perfume Saint"), who materializes rose perfume onto his palm from a distance, then jasmine perfume into a scentless flower, without touching him. Yogananda tests the phenomenon on sister Uma, who smells the jasmine from a flower she knows to be scentless. The chapter includes a footnote (FN5-5) explaining Gandha Baba's method: he tuned himself with "cosmic force" and guided "lifetrons" (subtle life energies) to rearrange vibratory structures and objectivize desired results. Yogananda judges perfume miracles "spectacular but spiritually useless."

**Chapter 6—The Tiger Swami (Sohong Swami)**: Yogananda and friend Chandi visit the famed Tiger Swami at Bhowanipur. The swami is immensely muscular, unclothed save a tiger skin, with "flowing locks, beard and moustache." He explains he once fought tigers with his bare hands: "You look upon tigers as tigers; I know them as pussycats." He recounts his story: he was once frail as a child but overcame by willing thoughts of health and strength. Fame brought pride; he performed tiger-fighting publicly. His father warned him of a saint's prediction: "Your next tiger-encounter shall result in your severe wounds, followed by six months of deathly sickness." He was challenged by the Prince of Cooch Behar to fight Raja Begum, a savage tiger. He won—binding the tiger with a chain while both were bloodied—but suffered wounds and blood poisoning for six months. A saint then appeared and initiated him: "Enough of tiger taming. Come with me; I will teach you to subdue the beasts of ignorance roaming in jungles of the human mind."

**Chapter 7—The Levitating Saint (Nagendra Nath Bhaduri)**: Friend Upendra Mohun Chowdhury tells Yogananda he saw Bhaduri Mahasaya levitate at a group meeting. Yogananda visits Bhaduri at his cloister on Upper Circular Road; the saint rarely leaves home, only sometimes visiting his front sidewalk during festivals. Yogananda describes Bhaduri's bhastrika pranayama ("such amazing force that it seemed an actual storm had arisen in the room") and his levitation. Bhaduri explains he has lived indoors for twenty years. He wears only a loincloth, sits in lotus, and has an "aura of peace after the storm" after meditation. He corresponds with American societies interested in yoga. When Yogananda asks him to write a book, Bhaduri replies: "I am training disciples. They and their students will be living volumes, proof against the natural disintegrations of time and the unnatural interpretations of the critics." He recites a song by Mirabai: "If by bathing daily God could be realized, / Sooner would I be a whale in the deep." Visitors place rupees in his slippers. He tells Yogananda that India is young, that Vedic wisdom "suffices for this day and land." Yogananda continues visiting after Bhaduri moves to Ram Mohan Roy Road (Nagendra Math). The chapter ends with Bhaduri's farewell words before Yogananda's departure for the West: "Son, go to America. Take the dignity of hoary India for your shield. Victory is written on your brow."

**Chapter 8—India's Great Scientist, Jagadis Chandra Bose**: Yogananda overhears professors discussing how Bose's wireless inventions antedated Marconi's. He visits Bose at his home near Gurpar Road. Bose describes his crescograph, "ten million magnifications," showing plants have nervous systems and emotional lives. At the Bose Institute dedication, Bose delivers a speech likening the institute to "a temple" and himself to one who found boundary lines vanishing "between the realms of the living and the non-living." He describes metal fatigue, plant responses to chloroform and antidotes, and the discovery that sap ascent involves living cells with a "peristaltic wave" from a "cylindrical tube" acting as "an actual heart." The chapter includes extensive footnotes on Sanskrit linguistics, Vaisesika atomism, and Emerson's tribute to Vedic thought. Bose's quote from Tagore's poem is included: "O Hermit, call thou in the authentic words / Of that old hymn called SAMA; 'Rise! Awake!'"

**Chapter 9—The Blissful Devotee and His Cosmic Romance (Master Mahasaya)**: Yogananda visits Master Mahasaya at 50 Amherst Street—the very house where his mother died. Master Mahasaya is "angelic" with "silky white beard and large lustrous eyes," seated in prayer. Yogananda feels an "agony at separation from my Divine Mother" and collapses at the saint's feet, begging his intercession. Master promises to "make your plea to the Beloved." The next night at ten o'clock, Yogananda has a vision of the Divine Mother, haloed in splendor, saying "Always have I loved thee! Ever shall I love thee!" He returns to Master Mahasaya the next morning; he guesses correctly that the Mother had spoken to him at ten o'clock, proving his clairvoyance. Master Mahasaya says "I am not your guru; he shall come a little later"—referring to Sri Yukteswar. He is a disciple of Sri Ramakrishna Paramhansa. Yogananda recounts pilgrimages to Dakshineswar Temple with him, sitting in a tamarisk grove during which Master Mahasaya chants and Yogananda soars in a "supernal visit." Another day, Master Mahasaya arranges that a tedious lecturer's hall lights go out until they can leave, and that a tiresome talker's thoughts are redirected by Divine Mother to make him leave a red house gate. He takes Yogananda to a bioscope (movie theater) but then, on the sidewalk, slaps Yogananda's chest and the world becomes silent: pedestrians and vehicles move noiselessly, Yogananda's body is shadow among shadows, friends pass without recognition, "a mellow luminescence permeated the panoramic view." Master slaps his chest again and sound returns. The saint calls this "bioscope," noting his master (Ramakrishna) told him to meditate "whenever I saw an expanse of water."

**Chapter 10—I Meet My Master, Sri Yukteswar**: Yogananda passes his high school finals after a friend, Nantu, coaches him, and after he finds Sanskrit verse on discarded sheets that enable him to pass the Sanskrit exam. He decides to join a Mahamandal hermitage in Benares with friend Jitendra Mazumdar. At the ashram, head swami Dyananda gives him rules: return Father's money, and "even when you feel hunger, don't mention it." Yogananda suffers a 24-hour fast, then Dyananda's train is late, so another meal is delayed. When Dyananda arrives, he reveals he has spent four days without food and "never eats on trains." He tells Yogananda: "Die then! . . . Never admit that you live by the power of food. . . . Do not imagine that rice maintains you." At the ashram, Yogananda's amulet vanishes (fulfilling the sadhu's prophecy). After three weeks of hostility, Dyananda leaves for a conference, and Yogananda is accused of being "a parasite." He decides to leave and seek his guru. He prays: "Merciful Mother of the Universe, teach me Thyself through visions, or through a guru sent by Thee!" A voice answers: "Thy Master cometh today!" A servant calls him to an errand. He goes to the market with Habu, and in a narrow lane he sees a Christlike man in ocher robes—Sri Yukteswar Giri. "Gurudeva!" Yogananda falls at his feet. Sri Yukteswar says: "O my own, you have come to me! How many years I have waited for you!" He takes Yogananda to his temporary residence in Rana Mahal, Benares, overlooking the Ganges. He says: "I will give you my hermitages and all I possess" and "I give you my unconditional love." He asks for Yogananda's unconditional love in return, explaining ordinary love is "selfish" but "divine love is without condition, without boundary, without change." He warns: "You will come to me in four weeks. . . . The next time we meet, you will have to reawaken my interest: I won't accept you as a disciple easily."
